alt="BeanBot screenshot" style="max-width:100%;"> > [[Onboarding]] > [[Pick Your Harness]] To understand what the AI already knows about your code, read [[Automatic Context Capture]].<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Opening the Mini Assistant</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> There are several ways to launch it: * **Toolbar button:** Click the **Mini Assistant** icon (a small chat bubble) in the assistant toolbar. This will open the mini dialog alongside the main panel. * **Keyboard shortcut:** Press `Ctrl + Alt + L` (or `Cmd + Alt + L` on Mac) to toggle it. * **Refactoring menu:** Right-click in the editor and choose **Ask Assistant** from the Refactoring menu. * **Code generation:** Press `Alt + Insert` (or the code generation shortcut for your platform) and select **Ask Assistant**. > [[Mini Assistant]] > [[Using the Mini Assistant]] > [[Keyboard shortcuts inside the Mini Assistant]] > [[Mini Assistant Permission Requests]] > [[Differences from the main panel]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Using the Mini Assistant</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> The dialog has a simple layout: a response display area on top and a text input at the bottom. Type your message and press `Enter` to send. Use `Shift + Enter` to add a newline without sending. While the AI is processing, a spinner and a token counter appear in the header so you can see progress in real time. The latest response is displayed as a compact bubble with a reduced font size. > [[Mini Assistant]] > [[Opening the Mini Assistant]] > [[Keyboard shortcuts inside the Mini Assistant]] > [[Mini Assistant Permission Requests]] > [[Differences from the main panel]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Keyboard shortcuts inside the Mini Assistant</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <table class="ug-table"> <thead><tr><th>Shortcut</th><th>Action</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr><td><code>Enter</code></td><td>Send message</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Shift + Enter</code></td><td>New line</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Tab</code></td><td>Slash command autocomplete</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Page Up / Page Down</code></td><td>Navigate between response bubbles</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Ctrl + C</code></td><td>Copy code block or full text</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Ctrl + L</code></td><td>Toggle the main assistant panel</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Ctrl + Alt + L</code></td><td>Toggle the mini assistant itself</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Escape</code></td><td>Close popups, then close the dialog</td></tr> </tbody> </table> When you navigate away from the latest bubble using Page Up/Down, auto-tracking pauses until you return to the newest response. > [[Mini Assistant]] > [[Opening the Mini Assistant]] > [[Using the Mini Assistant]] > [[Mini Assistant Permission Requests]] > [[Differences from the main panel]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Mini Assistant Permission Requests</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> If the AI requests permission to edit a file or run a command, the permission prompt appears directly inside the mini dialog. You can Allow or Deny the request, and for file edits, a **Show Diff** button lets you inspect the changes before approving. The buttons keep the same keyboard mnemonics as the main panel — <code>Alt + A</code> Always Allow, <code>Alt + O</code> Allow Once, <code>Alt + R</code> Reject/Deny, <code>Alt + W</code> Always Reject and <code>Alt + D</code> Show Diff — so you can answer a prompt without leaving the keyboard. On a Mac use <code>Option</code> in place of <code>Alt</code>: both <code>Option + A</code> and <code>Ctrl + Option + A</code> answer the prompt, see [[Permission Requests]]. > [[Mini Assistant]] > [[Opening the Mini Assistant]] > [[Using the Mini Assistant]] > [[Keyboard shortcuts inside the Mini Assistant]] > [[Differences from the main panel]] > [[Permission Requests]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Differences from the main panel</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> The mini assistant is designed for quick interactions. Some slash commands that require the full options panel (`/model`, `/models`, `/agents`, `/level`, `/sessions`) are not available in the mini view — use the main panel or its keyboard shortcuts for those. The dialog remembers its position and size across sessions, so you can place it wherever is convenient in your workspace. > [[Mini Assistant]] > [[Opening the Mini Assistant]] > [[Using the Mini Assistant]] > [[Keyboard shortcuts inside the Mini Assistant]] > [[Mini Assistant Permission Requests]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Install Ollama</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> [Ollama](https://ollama.com) lets you run open-source models locally on your own machine. The first step is installing it. Download the installer for your operating system from the [Ollama website](https://ollama.com/download) and run it. On Linux you can also use the install script: <pre><code> curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh </code></pre> On macOS, Ollama installs as a regular app — launch it once so the background service starts. **Windows (10 or later)** is also supported: install via the standalone `OllamaSetup.exe` download, or run the PowerShell installer: <pre><code> irm https://ollama.com/install.ps1 | iex </code></pre> Verify the installation by opening a terminal (or PowerShell on Windows) and running: <pre><code> ollama --version </code></pre> Once the `ollama` command responds, move on to fetching a coding model. > [[Fetch a Coding Model]] > [[Offline/Private Coding (Local LLMs)]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Fetch a Coding Model</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> With Ollama installed, open a terminal and pull a model suited for code. Good options include: <pre><code> ollama pull deepseek-coder ollama pull qwen2.5-coder ollama pull codellama ollama pull llama3.1 </code></pre> The first run of `ollama run <model>` will download the model if it is not already present. You can see what is installed at any time with: <pre><code> ollama list </code></pre> Remember the exact model names shown by `ollama list` — you will need them when [[configuring OpenCode->Configure OpenCode for Ollama]]. > [[Install Ollama]] > [[Configure OpenCode for Ollama]] > [[Offline/Private Coding (Local LLMs)]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Configure OpenCode for Ollama</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> OpenCode needs to know which provider serves the local model. Open your `opencode.json` configuration file (see [[Configuration Template]] for where this file lives) and add an `ollama` entry to its `provider` section. The rest of your existing file — permissions, etc. — stays untouched, so it looks something like this: <pre><code> ` { "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "autoupdate": false, "permission": { ... }, "provider": { "ollama": { "npm": "@ai-sdk/ollama", "options": { "baseURL": "http://localhost:11434/api" }, "models": { "deepseek-coder": {}, "qwen2.5-coder": {} } } } } ` </code></pre> The `...` stands for whatever permissions and other settings your file already has — keep them, and add the `provider` block alongside them. The exact `models` entries must match the names shown by `ollama list` from the previous step. Qwen models may require `"reasoningEffort": "none"` and `--think=false` if they are configured via Ollama. Once the provider block is in place, select the model in the plugin. > [[Fetch a Coding Model]] > [[Select the Model in the Plugin]] > [[Configuration Template]] > [[Manage OpenCode Config in NetBeans]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Select the Model in the Plugin</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> After [[configuring OpenCode->Configure OpenCode for Ollama]], pick your local model in the plugin: 1. Click the gear icon (or press `Tab` in the input area) to open the chat options panel. 2. Pick the **agent** you want to use (e.g. `build` or `plan`). 3. Pick your **model** from the model dropdown — the local models configured above will appear there, listed as their provider/model names. 4. Choose a suitable **Thinking Level** if the model supports one. Every query and indexing task now runs entirely on your machine — no data leaves your computer. See [[Offline/Private Coding (Local LLMs)]] for privacy notes and [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] for more on the selectors. > [[Configure OpenCode for Ollama]] > [[Offline/Private Coding (Local LLMs)]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Options Panel Reference]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">MCP Tools</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> The plugin runs a small built-in MCP (Model Context Protocol) server inside the IDE and exposes it to the Harness. If the agent supports MCP, it can call a handful of NetBeans tools directly during your conversation — you don't have to switch to the IDE and click around: <table class="ug-table"> <thead><tr><th>Tool</th><th>What it does</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr><td><code>get&#95;tabs</code></td><td>Lists the file paths currently open in editor tabs (only files inside your open projects).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>get&#95;current&#95;file&#95;context</code></td><td>Returns the active editor's file path, cursor position, and selection — the same context that is automatically attached to each message.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>open&#95;pos</code></td><td>Opens a file at a given line number. When the AI navigates on its own — while reading or writing files — it opens <em>in the background</em>: the caret moves to that line, but focus stays wherever you are working. When you ask to be taken somewhere ("show me where this happens", "take me to line 42"), the AI passes <code>focus=true</code> and the editor is brought to the front and focused.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>list&#95;projects</code></td><td>Lists the absolute paths of all open NetBeans projects.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>rename&#95;session</code></td><td>Gives the current (or a specific) session a custom title, just like the rename button.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>add&#95;task</code></td><td>Creates a task in a BeanBot Tasks repository. Accepts summary, status, priority (A–Z), tags, projects, due date, estimate, and consumed. See [[Adding Tasks via AI]].</td></tr> <tr><td><code>diff&#95;stash</code></td><td>Opens the side-by-side stash diff viewer for a given stash. Only available when Stash Diff is enabled in Options.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>read&#95;file</code> / <code>write&#95;to&#95;file</code></td><td>Reads or writes a file inside one of your open projects. <code>write&#95;to&#95;file</code> can create missing parent directories.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>replace&#95;lines</code> / <code>insert&#95;in&#95;file</code> / <code>delete&#95;lines</code></td><td>Line-range edits inside project files: replace a range, insert before a line, or delete a range (both 1-indexed, end inclusive).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>list&#95;directory</code></td><td>Lists files and subdirectories of a project directory, optionally recursively.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>search&#95;project</code></td><td>Searches project files for a text pattern or regex, with an optional glob filter and subdirectory restriction.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>find&#95;java&#95;type</code></td><td>Finds Java types by name across your open projects, like Navigate &gt; Go to Type, and returns fully qualified names and source paths. Java only — types from other languages are not searched.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>run&#95;command</code></td><td>Executes a shell command in the current session's working directory (or a specified directory). Returns stdout, stderr, merged output, and exit code. Each output stream is capped at 1 MB; when truncated, the result marks it with <code>truncated: true</code>. Timed-out commands return any partial output collected before the timeout. The working directory must be inside an open project for security.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>git&#95;status</code> / <code>git&#95;diff</code> / <code>git&#95;log</code></td><td>Runs git status (short form), git diff (unstaged, staged, or a specific revision), or git log from an open project's repository — not a parent checkout above the project.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>file&#95;history</code></td><td>Commit history of a single file in that git repository, including each version's patch.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>hg&#95;status</code> / <code>hg&#95;diff</code> / <code>hg&#95;log</code></td><td>Same operations for Mercurial, from an open project's <code>.hg</code> repository.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>hg&#95;file&#95;hist</code></td><td>Commit history of a single file in that Mercurial repository.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>update&#95;task</code> / <code>close&#95;task</code> / <code>search&#95;task</code></td><td>Change, complete, or find tasks in a BeanBot Tasks repository. See [[Adding Tasks via AI]].</td></tr> </tbody> </table> All filesystem, git, and Mercurial tools are confined to your currently open projects — paths outside them (including symlinks that point outside) are rejected. A failed git or hg command is reported as an error, not a successful tool result. The MCP server binds to <code>127.0.0.1</code> and verifies a per-instance token, so it never accepts connections from outside your machine; the token is appended to the server URL handed to your Harness. The one exception is a Harness that cannot carry a token on an MCP URL — a Pi-family binary (<code>pi</code>, <code>pi-acp</code>, <code>pi-agent</code>) or Jcode (<code>jcode</code>) — see [[PI Agent]] and [[Jcode Agent]] — which connects without one. The server port can be fixed in Options (BeanBot > System); by default the OS picks a random free port. It only activates when your Harness advertises MCP support. When the AI uses one of these tools, the call and its result appear in the chat as a collapsible tool bubble with the tag icon — same as any other tool output. > [[Thinking and Tool Responses]] > [[Git Stashes as "Code Drafts" (using Stash Diff)]] > [[Renaming the session]] > [[Automatic Context Capture]] > [[Adding Tasks via AI]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Automatic Context Capture</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> Every message you send automatically carries supplementary context about your current editor state, so the AI knows what you are working on without you having to explain it. For the active editor this includes: - the file path of the open document - the selected text and its line range, when you have a selection - the current cursor line Your active project is attached as well, so the AI knows the boundaries of your project. This context is reference-only metadata — your typed message is always the primary input. If no real file is open (for example an empty editor or a temporary document), no phantom path like <code>/tmp/xxx</code> is sent, so the AI is never confused by made-up file locations. The MCP <code>open&#95;pos</code> and <code>get&#95;tabs</code> tools let the AI jump you to the exact file and line it is talking about. > [[Home]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Chat Features]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Reloading a Session</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> The **Reload** button (reload icon) on the toolbar re-fetches the current session from the server. Your messages are always stored on the server, so reloading never loses anything — it just refreshes the chat view to match the server state. You'll want to reload when: - you ran <code>/compact</code> and want the summarised history displayed - older messages were trimmed from the view (click **Show All Messages** first, then **Reload** to bring them all back) - the view seems out of sync with the server, for example after a server restart or a session reload from the dropdown > [[Message History]] > [[Resetting context limits (/compact)]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Restarting the server]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Welcome Screen</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> When the assistant panel is opened with no session selected, you'll see the welcome screen instead of a chat thread. Click the **New Session** button (green plus icon) on the toolbar to begin a new conversation. <img alt="Welcome Screen Toolbar" style="max-width:100%;"> > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Session Dropdown Menu]] > [[Archiving Sessions]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Auto-Reconnect</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> If the server process dies or its connection breaks mid-conversation, the plugin handles it automatically: 1. any stale server process is killed and its connections closed 2. a notification appears: **Harness Disconnected — Attempting to reconnect...** 3. the server is restarted automatically with a short backoff (about 3, 6, then 9 seconds) The plugin gives up after **3 failed restarts within 5 minutes** and shows a "server crashed" status message. In that case check your installation, then click **Restart Harness** to try again. Your sessions are not lost during a reconnect — they are stored on the server and simply reloaded. > [[Restarting the server]] > [[Onboarding]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Expand/Collapse All</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <img src="data:image/webp;base64,UklGRmQCAABXRUJQVlA4TFcCAAAvUIALAE/ksG0bSVKa2Pa3yL03O7Hu7cFhI0lONJd/EIj84L1Z1kw7aCPJkWr4g3iQ+Sd0zf863H6fAAUQAKAAQAIoAAQAW6CUHE1ErqMAAAiScpQJjMnQmN8RYGUEEmA8j7HiAECTwgAoAfq++rMKZAIwoblCh6208pfWZGgBABo6ACkBUgIJAAAAKiWgUgILpYJKqZRKqZTKg69tR61Sq3Q2UWebOSLRWaOzzRxRHNfvWxyd7Xg/iUSP+IlDdNYQiVavOER/9u1BJJo538fMWb0e8SPqbKvX/f8lEkG2bdumHc3Ytm3bLsRcsW2fnLVi67uv9jm1yy8R/Z+AV+3if/4lFuW8ZIF3gBWnYuGxBVVfkiyYF5HzU4XnIjKvzL+67/u3dHVX2yyLULjAvH2tKqSBqJf6M5Xh8ljMD8/eTTm+hOLgTqLhxl6iEmV4EzafPHm6YH6D4vjuXuqJQekwjVQqw4wh+57sizEDxcmj1NsSCaCgn/prvVRhk3nDvQ3mTShvomYfOGYNUi6U3x6yTLozJXx4p863yA/OU1Jh4eO5GC+ung05f8QPP2PI3rWz630xZqHBFeYtZ1vMq9DhzS7znMMc8+6NFnB/JvwKvLKc30OTn8w7wA7LB7TJcgQcikAnB8CBDeJchYVqInssw1lQfXuEFvL7iYodAjuIesN1gLJhGqkAYrt66WsCtIDCfhqoSRui3rYoaAI5g0S9RK2+0AYSx4kG6/xgvSmyfmUPRHdNlMOOa4aYJ4Y94JUHW159mixiExsvH5pyoRc8LB1Pa+ZvKgA=" alt="Expand/Collapse All button" style="max-width:100%;"> Thoughts, tool outputs and code blocks are rendered as collapsible panes so a long assistant response stays readable. Instead of opening or closing them one by one, use the **Expand/Collapse All** toolbar button to toggle every block in the chat at once. The button icon and tooltip switch between *Expand All* and *Collapse All* so you always know what the next click will do. It's handy right after streaming finishes — collapse everything to see the final summary, or expand everything to inspect every tool result. > [[Thinking and Tool Responses]] > [[Keyboard Shortcuts]] > [[Filtering Chat Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Keyboard Shortcuts Dialog</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> Click the keyboard icon in the assistant panel header to open the **Keyboard Shortcuts** dialog. It lists every shortcut the plugin supports, grouped by section — Navigation &amp; Assistant, Session Management, Chat Input, Editing and Stash Diff — with the keys rendered as keyboard badges. Type in the filter field at the top to search by key or action name. Shortcuts that are not currently assigned are collapsed into a single clickable *Unassigned* summary row per section; click it to expand the full list. Press <code>Escape</code> to close the dialog. > [[Keyboard Shortcuts]] > [[Customising the Toolbar]] > [[Input Area Keys]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Global Configuration Setup</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> The first time you start the IDE (and on server restarts), if you are using OpenCode as the harness, the plugin checks for a global OpenCode configuration file at `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (or `opencode.jsonc`). This file holds security settings like file-permission rules and which commands require your approval. If the file is missing, empty, or contains only the `$schema` reference, the chat panel shows a prompt offering to write a starter configuration: * **Set up starter config** — writes the bundled starter file (see [[Configuration Template]]) to your config directory. * **Not now** — defers the prompt for the current IDE session. It won't ask again until you restart the IDE. If an existing file can't be parsed, the prompt instead asks whether to **Replace** it (which overwrites the broken file) or **Keep** it unchanged. Files that already contain real configuration are never touched. When a config prompt was shown, a confirmation hint with an **OK** button appears before the server starts — click it to proceed. The hint also points you to `opencode auth login` and the free models at **Opencode Zen** (https://opencode.ai/docs/zen/) if you haven't added a model provider yet. > [[Configuration Template]] > [[Manage OpenCode Config in NetBeans]] > [[Onboarding]] > [[Post Install]] > [[Restarting the server]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Task Repositories</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> BeanBot integrates with the NetBeans Tasks Dashboard to let you manage tasks alongside your code. Each <b>task repository</b> maps to a plain todo.txt file on disk — readable and editable with any standard todo.txt tool (see the <a href="https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt" target="_blank">todo.txt spec</a>). To get started, create a repository — see [[Creating a Task Repository]]. Once registered, your tasks appear in the NetBeans Tasks Dashboard — see [[Using the Tasks Dashboard]]. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Multiple repositories</div> You can register multiple repositories (e.g. one per project). When adding a task via the AI, specify the repository by name; if only one exists it is used automatically. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Repository name</div> The task repository appears as <b>BeanBot</b> in the NetBeans bugtracking UI (the "Report a New Task" page). This is the connector display name — distinct from the repository's display name, which you set when creating it. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Adding tasks with the AI</div> You can also create tasks conversationally by asking BeanBot to add a task — it uses the built-in <code>add&#95;task</code> MCP tool. See [[Adding Tasks via AI]] for details. > [[Creating a Task Repository]] > [[Using the Tasks Dashboard]] > [[Todo.txt Format]] > [[Adding Tasks via AI]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Todo.txt Format</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> BeanBot stores tasks as plain todo.txt files — one task per line (see the <a href="https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt" target="_blank">todo.txt spec</a>). The format extends the spec with a small set of BeanBot-specific tokens. Because it's plain text, you can edit your tasks with any todo.txt tool, a text editor, or version control. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Line layout</div> <pre>x (B) 2026-08-02 2026-08-01 Fix the bug @urgent @bug +myproject due:2026-09-01 id:t-1a2b3c4d estimate:5 consumed:2 upd:2026-08-02T10:00:00Z</pre> <table class="ug-table"> <thead><tr><th>Token</th><th>Meaning</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr><td><code>x </code> (optional prefix)</td><td>Marks the task <b>closed</b>. Its absence means <b>open</b> — there is no <code>status:</code> token.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>(A)</code>–<code>(Z)</code></td><td>Priority letter. Placed immediately after <code>x </code> (or as the first token when open). Native todo.txt syntax.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>YYYY-MM-DD</code> (first date)</td><td>Completion date — only present when the task is closed (<code>x </code>).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>YYYY-MM-DD</code> (second date)</td><td>Creation date — present for both open and closed tasks.</td></tr> <tr><td><i>free text</i></td><td>The task summary. Preserved verbatim on save.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>@word</code></td><td>A <b>tag</b> (e.g. <code>@urgent</code>).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>+word</code></td><td>A <b>project</b> (e.g. <code>+myproject</code>).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>due:YYYY-MM-DD</code></td><td>Due date — a standard todo.txt extension.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>id:t-XXXXXXXX</code></td><td>Stable task id. If missing, BeanBot generates one in NetBeans format.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>estimate:&lt;int&gt;</code></td><td>Estimated effort in arbitrary user-inferred units.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>consumed:&lt;int&gt;</code></td><td>Consumed effort in the same units.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>upd:&lt;iso&gt;</code></td><td>Last-modified timestamp (full ISO-8601).</td></tr> </tbody> </table> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Priority letters</div> BeanBot uses the full A–Z range for priority. In the task editor, priorities are shown as NATO phonetic words (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie … Zulu) but stored as single uppercase letters. A is the highest priority; N (November) is the default. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Tags and projects</div> Tags and projects are stored <b>only</b> as <code>@</code> and <code>+</code> tokens — there is no redundant <code>tags:</code> or <code>projects:</code> mirror. This ensures a load→save round-trip never duplicates them. Tags appear in the dashboard's tag filter; projects are a separate dimension for grouping. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Estimate and consumed</div> <code>estimate</code> and <code>consumed</code> are integers representing <b>arbitrary, user-defined units</b> — BeanBot does not assign them meaning. They are for personal tracking only (e.g. story points, hours, t-shirt sizes). <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">External tool compatibility</div> Unknown tokens are tolerated on read and ignored, so files edited by other todo.txt tools remain compatible. Lines without a parseable task (e.g. blank lines) are skipped. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Reserialization safety</div> When BeanBot reads a task file and writes it back, it preserves: <ul> <li>The summary text byte-for-byte (no reformatting).</li> <li>All <code>@</code>/<code>+</code> tokens exactly as read.</li> <li>All <code>key:value</code> tokens (id, estimate, consumed, upd, due).</li> <li>The positional dates and priority letter.</li> </ul> This means external edits survive a BeanBot save without spurious diffs. > [[Task Repositories]] > alt="Task Editor" style="max-width:100%;"> The task editor opens when you create or edit a task from the NetBeans Tasks Dashboard or via the assistant toolbar. It has two sections separated by a divider. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Top section — Summary, Tags, Projects</div> <table class="ug-table"> <thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr><td><b>Summary*</b></td><td>The task title (required). Shows a grey placeholder ("Enter summary") when empty.</td></tr> <tr><td><b>Tags</b></td><td>Chip-based editor for <code>@</code>-prefixed tags. Type a tag and press Enter, or pick from the dropdown. Predefined: bug, documentation, duplicate, enhancement, feedback, home, invalid, wontfix, work.</td></tr> <tr><td><b>Projects</b></td><td>Chip-based editor for <code>+</code>-prefixed projects. The dropdown is pre-populated with your currently open NetBeans project names (spaces replaced with hyphens).</td></tr> </tbody> </table> Tags and projects are shown as removable pills. Click the <b>x</b> on a pill to remove it. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Bottom section — Status, Priority, Estimate, Consumed</div> <table class="ug-table"> <thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr><td><b>Status</b></td><td>Open or closed. Defaults to open.</td></tr> <tr><td><b>Priority</b></td><td>A–Z letter, shown as NATO phonetic words (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie … Zulu). November (N) is the default.</td></tr> <tr><td><b>Estimate</b></td><td>Arbitrary effort units (integer). Defaults to 0.</td></tr> <tr><td><b>Consumed</b></td><td>Arbitrary effort units consumed so far (integer). Defaults to 0.</td></tr> </tbody> </table> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Due dates</div> Due dates are managed via the dashboard's native <b>Schedule</b> submenu (right-click a task &gt; Schedule), not through the task editor. The editor preserves any existing due date rather than exposing one. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Saving</div> The editor uses the bugtracking framework's standard save mechanism — changes are saved when you close the editor and confirm, or when the framework auto-saves. There is no explicit Save button in the form. > [[Task Repositories]] > [[Using the Tasks Dashboard]] > [[Todo.txt Format]] > [[Adding Tasks via AI]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Adding Tasks via AI</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> You can create tasks conversationally by asking BeanBot to add one. The assistant uses the built-in <code>add&#95;task</code> MCP tool to write directly to your task repository. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.4em; margin-bottom: 0;">Example prompts</div> <ul style="margin-top: 0; margin-bottom: 0.2em;"> <li style="margin-bottom: 0.2em;"><i>"Add a task to fix the login bug"</i></li> <li style="margin-bottom: 0.2em;"><i>"Create a high-priority task: refactor the database layer"</i></li> <li><i>"Track a task: write unit tests for the parser, estimate 3 points"</i></li> </ul> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">What you can specify</div> <table class="ug-table"> <thead><tr><th>Parameter</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr><td><code>summary</code></td><td>The task title (required).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>status</code></td><td><code>open</code> or <code>closed</code>. Defaults to open.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>priority</code></td><td>A single uppercase letter A–Z.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>tags</code></td><td>Comma-separated tags (stored as <code>@tag</code> in the file).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>projects</code></td><td>Comma-separated project names (stored as <code>+project</code> in the file).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>dueDate</code></td><td>ISO-8601 date string.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>estimate</code></td><td>Integer (arbitrary effort units).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>consumed</code></td><td>Integer (effort consumed so far).</td></tr> </tbody> </table> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Repository selection</div> If you have multiple task repositories, specify which one to add to: <ul> <li><i>"Add a task to the Backend repo: fix the cache invalidation"</i></li> <li><i>"In the Frontend project, create a task to update the login form"</i></li> </ul> If only one repository exists, it is used automatically. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0;">Updating, closing, and finding tasks</div> <ul style="margin-top: 0; margin-bottom: 0.2em;"> <li style="margin-bottom: 0.2em;"><i>"Rename task t-3 to fix the cache"</i> — <code>update&#95;task</code></li> <li style="margin-bottom: 0.2em;"><i>"Mark the login-bug task as done"</i> — <code>close&#95;task</code></li> <li><i>"Which open tasks mention login?"</i> — <code>search&#95;task</code> (open tasks only, up to 10 matches)</li> </ul> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">How it works</div> The <code>add&#95;task</code> tool creates a new task in the repository's in-memory cache, persists it to the `todo.txt` file (in a background thread), and returns the task id. <code>update&#95;task</code> and <code>close&#95;task</code> change an existing row the same way. The task then appears in the NetBeans Tasks Dashboard immediately. > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Task Repositories]] > [[Task Editor]] > [[Todo.txt Format]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Creating a Task Repository</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> Each BeanBot task repository maps to a plain todo.txt file on disk. Creating one takes a few clicks: <ol> <li>Go to <b>Tools &gt; Options &gt; Miscellaneous &gt; Tasks</b> (the BeanBot Tasks options panel).</li> <li>Click <b>Add</b> and fill in: <ul> <li><b>Display name</b> — a human-readable label (defaults to your current project name).</li> <li><b>Tasks file</b> — the path to the <code>.txt</code> file. Defaults to <code>beanbot&#95;todo.txt</code> in the project root.</li> </ul></li> <li>Click <b>OK</b>. The repository is registered and its file is loaded (or created if it doesn't exist yet).</li> </ol> You can register multiple repositories (e.g. one per project). Each repository is remembered across IDE restarts; the underlying todo.txt file is user-maintained and never moved by the plugin. Once created, your tasks appear in the NetBeans Tasks Dashboard — see [[Using the Tasks Dashboard]]. > [[Task Repositories]] > [[Using the Tasks Dashboard]] > [[Todo.txt Format]]<div style="display: alt="Using the Tasks Dashboard" style="max-width:100%;"> Once a repository is registered, your tasks appear in the NetBeans <b>Tasks Dashboard</b> (Window &gt; Tasks). You can: <ul> <li><b>Create tasks</b> via the dashboard's "New Task" button or from the assistant's toolbar.</li> <li><b>Edit tasks</b> by double-clicking them — the task editor opens with Summary, Status, Priority, Tags, Projects, Estimate, and Consumed fields. See [[Task Editor]].</li> <li><b>Set due dates</b> via the dashboard's Schedule submenu (right-click a task &gt; Schedule).</li> <li><b>Filter by tags</b> using the Find Tasks query dialog.</li> </ul> The dashboard's Open / Finished grouping follows the task status: tasks marked closed (the todo.txt <code>x </code> prefix) appear under Finished; everything else is Open. Tasks can also be created conversationally via the AI — see [[Adding Tasks via AI]]. > [[Task Repositories]] > [[Task Editor]] > [[Adding Tasks via AI]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Queuing Messages</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> On agents that drop an in-flight prompt if you send another (see below), you don't have to wait for the assistant to finish before typing. While the agent is working (Go/Stop button shows the running state), anything you send is <b>queued</b> instead of interrupting the current turn. When the turn ends, all queued messages are combined into a single prompt and sent automatically. No chat bubbles appear while messages are queued — a single bubble for the combined text is drawn when it is actually sent. The queue button appears on the toolbar with a brief amber flash on the first message, then wobbles periodically while more messages accumulate: <ul> <li><b>Send Now</b> — open the queue button's popup menu to flush the queued messages immediately, without waiting for the turn to end.</li> <li><b>Cancel Queue</b> — discard all queued messages.</li> </ul> Queueing is used when BeanBot must not send a second <code>session/prompt</code> into the running turn. That is currently [[Goose Agent]], [[PI Agent]], [[Hermes Agent]], [[OpenClaw Agent]], [[Codex Agent]], [[Kilo Code Agent]], [[Cline Agent]], and [[Jcode Agent]]. Interleaved agents ([[OpenCode]], [[Oh My Pi Agent]], [[Cursor Agent]], [[Copilot Agent]], [[Claude Agent]], [[Gemini Agent]], [[Devin Agent]]) send immediately instead. If you close or switch sessions before the turn ends, pending messages are cancelled with the rest of the panel state. > [[Chat Features]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Auto-Backup on Turn Start]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">PI Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice. The harness chooser labels Pi <b>Limited</b>; see [[Onboarding]].</i> <a href="https://pi.dev" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Pi</a> is a minimal, extensible **agent harness** — an open-source coding agent CLI built around a unified multi-provider LLM API, an agent runtime with tool calling, and a self-extensible extension system. It deliberately ships no built-in permission system: it runs with the permissions of the user who launched it, so sandbox or containerize it yourself if you need stronger boundaries. To use Pi with BeanBot, install the harness, then the ACP adapter: #### Install Install the harness first (Node.js 22+): <pre><code>npm install -g @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent</code></pre> BeanBot drives Pi through the <code>@geohar/pi-acp</code> adapter — a fork of <code>svkozak/pi-acp</code> that adds the subagent bridge, MCP handling, and multi-root workspaces. It needs <code>pi</code> 0.80.4+ on your <code>PATH</code>: <pre><code>npm install -g @geohar/pi-acp</code></pre> Loading it into Pi as an extension as well is optional — it surfaces the pi-subagents fleet as tasks in the chat: <pre><code>pi install npm:@geohar/pi-acp</code></pre> The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>pi-acp</code> (the adapter, not <code>pi</code> itself). When the session starts, Pi posts a startup banner with its version, context files and extensions, which the plugin renders as a compact info card. The plugin's [[MCP Tools]] reach Pi over ACP: BeanBot passes its MCP server in the session create/load request, and <code>@geohar/pi-acp</code> forwards it to Pi. One setup step remains: - **MCP adapter** — install <a href="https://github.com/nicobailon/pi-mcp-adapter" target="_blank" rel="noopener">pi-mcp-adapter</a> in your Pi packages. The adapter translates the ACP session's servers into a session-scoped config that it hands to Pi via <code>--mcp-config</code>; without it the servers are not loaded and Pi prints a startup notice. No manual <code>mcp.json</code> entry and no fixed port are needed — the server URL is delivered per session. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Goose Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> <a href="https://goose-docs.ai/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Goose</a> is an open-source, general-purpose **AI agent harness** from the Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation). It ships as a native desktop app, a CLI, and an embeddable API — all built in Rust — and works with 15+ LLM providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, OpenRouter, Bedrock, …). Goose speaks the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a> natively, and connects to 70+ extensions via the <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Model Context Protocol</a>. Install the CLI, then configure <code>goose</code> as the Harness in Options (BeanBot > Assistant Service) — make sure the binary is on your <code>PATH</code> or specify the full path. What works with Goose in BeanBot: - **[[Queuing Messages]]** — while Goose is working, your messages are queued and combined into one prompt at turn end (Goose, Pi, Hermes, and Oh My Pi all need this; interleaved agents send immediately). - **[[MCP Tools]]** — the plugin hands Goose a token-protected MCP server URL; the AI can read files, navigate the editor, and run git or Mercurial commands from the conversation. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Queuing Messages]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Hermes Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Install</div> - **macOS / Linux**: <pre><code>curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash</code></pre> - **Windows**: <pre><code>irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1 | iex</code></pre> After installing, enable ACP support: <pre><code>cd ~/.hermes/hermes-agent uv pip install -e '.&#91;acp&#93;'</code></pre> Requires Python 3.10+. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">About</div> <a href="https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Hermes</a> is an open-source **AI agent harness** from Nous Research. It is a Python-based coding agent with built-in tool calling, multi-provider LLM support, and a self-extensible plugin system. Hermes speaks the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a> natively, which is what BeanBot uses to drive it. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>hermes</code>. When the session starts, Hermes reports its available models and modes as structured fields — the plugin uses these to populate the Model and Mode dropdowns automatically. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">OpenCode</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <a href="https://opencode.ai" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OpenCode</a> is an open-source AI coding agent and the default harness for BeanBot. It supports 15+ LLM providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, OpenRouter, Bedrock, …) and speaks the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a> natively. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">macOS / Linux</div> <pre><code>curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash</code></pre> Or via package managers: - **npm**: <pre><code>npm install -g opencode-ai</code></pre> - **Homebrew**: <pre><code>brew install anomalyco/tap/opencode</code></pre> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Windows</div> On Windows, you can run OpenCode inside **WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)**, or use a package manager. To launch OpenCode through WSL from the plugin, enable **Launch through WSL** under `Tools > Options > BeanBot > Assistant Service`. The plugin detects `wsl.exe` on your PATH and wraps all OpenCode invocations through WSL automatically, translating your Windows executable path to its WSL mount location. <pre><code>curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash</code></pre> Or via package managers: - **Chocolatey**: <pre><code>choco install opencode</code></pre> - **Scoop**: <pre><code>scoop install opencode</code></pre> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Configuration</div> After installing, create the configuration file: <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">macOS / Linux</div> The config directory is at `$HOME/.config/opencode/`. <pre><code>mkdir -p &#36;HOME/.config/opencode</code></pre> Create `$HOME/.config/opencode/opencode.json` with the starter configuration: <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Windows</div> <pre><code> mkdir "%USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode" cd "%USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode" </code></pre> Open Notepad and paste in the starter configuration: > [[Configuration Template]] <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Verify</div> Run this to confirm the configuration is valid: <pre><code>opencode models</code></pre> Then proceed to [[Post Install]] to configure the plugin in NetBeans. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Options Panel Reference]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Pick Your Harness</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> BeanBot doesn't talk directly to AI services, it communicates via coding agents or harnesses, these applications interface with LLM providers like Anthropic or OpenAI, and provide authentication, persistence and context management. Most of them support a protocol called ACP or Agent Client Protocol that simplifies and standardises LLM access for IDEs and Editors, BeanBot takes advantage of this capability, we can connect to any provider or model as long as we find a suitable harness that speaks ACP. In this guide you might also see a harness referred to as an ACP Server, an Agent Server, or simply server, in the context of this plugin it's just a conduit for communicating with a remote LLM. These are the harnesses currently supported, pick the one you want to use. Even unlisted ones might work, but you have to experiment and find out. > [[OpenCode]] > [[Codex Agent]] > [[PI Agent]] > [[Goose Agent]] > [[Claude Agent]] > [[Cursor Agent]] > [[Copilot Agent]] > [[Hermes Agent]] > [[Gemini Agent]] > [[Oh My Pi Agent]] > [[OpenClaw Agent]] > [[Devin Agent]] > [[Kilo Code Agent]] > [[Cline Agent]] > [[Jcode Agent]] Some harnesses have **limited ACP support**: BeanBot can still connect and chat through them, but parts of the IDE integration are unavailable. The harness chooser (and the **Harness** dropdown under **Options > BeanBot**) labels those **Limited** — hover the badge or item to see exactly what is missing. Currently that is [[OpenClaw Agent]], [[Jcode Agent]], [[Gemini Agent]], [[PI Agent]] and [[Cline Agent]]; each page has the details. A harness's tier can change as its ACP support improves. If you are not sure, The plugin will detect installed harnesses and let you choose at startup. See [[Onboarding]]. > [[Home]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Claude Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Install</div> All platforms (requires Node.js 18+): <pre><code>npm install -g @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp</code></pre> The package bundles the Claude Agent SDK, so a separate `claude` CLI install is not needed. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">About</div> <a href="https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Claude Agent ACP</a> is an ACP adapter that exposes Claude's coding agent over the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a>, which is what BeanBot speaks. It supports session mode switching, MCP server injection, and editor context. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>claude-agent-acp</code>. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Cursor Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> #### Install - **macOS / Linux**: `curl https://cursor.com/install -fsSL | bash` - **Windows (PowerShell)**: `irm 'https://cursor.com/install?win32=true' | iex` Register once with the CLI (`agent login`, or set `CURSOR_API_KEY`) before connecting. #### About <a href="https://cursor.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cursor</a> is an AI-powered code editor with a built-in coding agent. Its CLI exposes an ACP entry point that BeanBot can drive. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>cursor-agent</code>. The ACP entry point is the CLI itself, run with `agent acp`. Cursor sends MCP server config and editor context automatically. Cursor is **interleaved**: you can send another message while a turn is still running. The new prompt is issued immediately (it is not held in the [[Queuing Messages]] toolbar queue). The previous request finishes as cancelled; the input stays busy until the latest prompt completes. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Queuing Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Gemini Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice. The harness chooser labels Gemini <b>Limited</b>; see [[Onboarding]].</i> #### About <a href="https://geminicli.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Gemini CLI</a> is an AI agent command-line tool. It natively supports communication with external tools using the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a>. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>gemini</code>, run with the default launch argument <code>--acp --model gemini-3.8-flash</code>. When you pick Gemini in the harness chooser or Options, BeanBot reminds you to change <code>--model</code> in Process Arguments if you want a different model. Gemini Agent in BeanBot supports: - [[Editor Context->Automatic Context Capture]] Seamlessly injects the active editor state into agent prompts. - **MCP Servers**: Automatically registers and injects the plug-in's [[MCP Tools]]. - **Client-Side Session Tracking**: Gemini CLI does not publish a session list, so BeanBot keeps session IDs on this machine. Sessions whose project is closed are hidden from the dropdown until that project is open again; IDs are kept so the chat can return. [[Archiving Sessions]] is local only. - **Interleaved prompts**: a new message is sent immediately (it does not wait in the [[Queuing Messages]] toolbar queue). See [[Cursor Agent]] for the same style. #### Model Selection Since Gemini CLI does not support changing the model dynamically via <code>session/set&#95;config&#95;option</code> once the session has started, you can configure your preferred model in one of three ways: 1. **Launch Arguments**: In the plugin options (<code>Tools > Options > BeanBot</code>, Process Arguments), set e.g. <code>--acp --model gemini-2.5-pro</code>. 2. **Settings File**: Define the default model in your global configuration file at <code>~/.gemini/settings.json</code>. 3. **Environment Variable**: Set the <code>GEMINI&#95;MODEL</code> environment variable before launching NetBeans. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Onboarding]] > [[Options Panel Reference]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Archiving Sessions]] > [[Queuing Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Oh My Pi Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> #### Install - **macOS / Linux**: `curl -fsSL https://omp.sh/install | sh` - **Windows (PowerShell)**: `irm https://omp.sh/install.ps1 | iex` - **Homebrew**: `brew install can1357/tap/omp` Then run <code>omp</code> in a terminal and use <code>/login</code> to authenticate a model provider. ACP docs: <a href="https://omp.sh/docs/acp" target="_blank" rel="noopener">omp.sh/docs/acp</a>. #### About **Oh My Pi (omp)** is an open-source, terminal-based AI coding agent forked from the Pi agent, designed to be a "batteries-included" version integrating full IDE-like capabilities into a terminal harness. Source: <a href="https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi" target="_blank" rel="noopener">can1357/oh-my-pi</a>. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>omp</code>, run with the default launch argument <code>acp</code>. Oh My Pi Agent in BeanBot supports: - [[Editor Context->Automatic Context Capture]] Seamlessly injects the active editor state into agent prompts. - **MCP Servers**: Automatically registers and injects the plug-in's [[MCP Tools]]. - **[[Queuing Messages]]**: Queues and batches user prompts at turn end. - **Session Management**: Supports full session lists and state persistence. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Onboarding]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Queuing Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">OpenClaw Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice. The harness chooser labels OpenClaw <b>Limited</b>; see [[Onboarding]].</i> #### Install - **macOS / Linux**: `curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash` - **Windows (PowerShell)**: `iwr -useb https://openclaw.ai/install.ps1 | iex` Requires **Node 24.16+ or 26.1+** — Node 26 is recommended, and the installer provisions Node when it is missing. ACP docs: <a href="https://docs.openclaw.ai/cli/acp" target="_blank" rel="noopener">docs.openclaw.ai/cli/acp</a>. #### About <a href="https://docs.openclaw.ai" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OpenClaw</a> is a personal AI assistant gateway. Running <code>openclaw acp</code> makes it act as an **ACP server**: the bridge speaks ACP over stdio, forwards each prompt to an OpenClaw **Gateway** over WebSocket, and maps each ACP session onto a Gateway session key. A running Gateway (local or remote) is required — the bridge routes work into it rather than hosting the agent itself. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>openclaw</code>, run with the default launch argument <code>acp</code>. OpenClaw Agent in BeanBot supports: - [[Editor Context->Automatic Context Capture]] Seamlessly injects the active editor state into agent prompts. - **[[Permission Requests]]**: Gateway exec-approval prompts during a turn are relayed into BeanBot's permission UI. - **Thinking Responses**: Model thinking streams into the chat as thought bubbles. - **[[Queuing Messages]]**: Queues and batches user prompts at turn end. - **Client-Side Session Tracking**: OpenClaw's ACP bridge accepts session-list requests but returns an empty list, so BeanBot keeps session IDs on this machine instead. Sessions whose project is closed are hidden from the dropdown until that project is open again; IDs are kept so the chat can return. [[Archiving Sessions]] is local only. #### Limitations OpenClaw runs as a **bridge** rather than a full ACP-native runtime, so a few ACP surfaces are unavailable: - **MCP Servers**: The bridge rejects per-session MCP servers, so BeanBot cannot hand OpenClaw the plugin's [[MCP Tools]] automatically — it sends no server list. OpenClaw still supports MCP: run the plugin's internal server on a fixed port (**Internal MCP Server** and **Internal MCP Server Port** under <code>Options &gt; BeanBot &gt; System</code>) and register that URL as a Gateway MCP server with <code>openclaw mcp add</code> (or <code>mcp.servers</code> in the OpenClaw config, or the Control UI's <code>/settings/mcp</code> page). The Gateway must run on the same machine, because the plugin's server binds to <code>127.0.0.1</code>. - **Model Selection**: Not exposed as an ACP config option, so the in-session model dropdown is unavailable. Change the model from within the chat with <code>/acp set model provider/model</code> — for example <code>/acp set model opencode-go/glm-5.3-flash</code>. - **Agent / Mode Dropdown**: OpenClaw routes by Gateway session key rather than advertising an agent list, so BeanBot does not offer the agent selector. To target a specific agent, add <code>--session agent:&lt;id&gt;:main</code> under Process Arguments in <code>Options &gt; BeanBot</code>. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Onboarding]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Queuing Messages]] > [[Archiving Sessions]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Devin Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> #### Install - **macOS / Linux / WSL**: `curl -fsSL https://cli.devin.ai/install.sh | bash` - **macOS (Homebrew)**: `brew install --cask devin-cli` - **Windows (PowerShell)**: `irm https://static.devin.ai/cli/setup.ps1 | iex` On Windows run that in **PowerShell** — `irm` and `iex` are PowerShell commands and fail in Git Bash or CMD. Afterwards <code>devin</code> works from PowerShell, Windows Terminal, or Git Bash. CLI docs: <a href="https://docs.devin.ai/cli" target="_blank" rel="noopener">docs.devin.ai/cli</a>. #### About <a href="https://docs.devin.ai/cli" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Devin CLI</a> is a local command-line coding agent, separate from cloud Devin. Running <code>devin acp</code> makes it act as an **ACP server** over stdio: it speaks JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout and is meant to be spawned by an ACP-aware editor, so it is not a command to run yourself. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>devin</code>, run with the default launch argument <code>acp</code>. **Authentication** is worth setting up before you connect: the ACP server reads credentials from the `WINDSURF_API_KEY` environment variable when it is set, and otherwise uses the credentials stored by <code>devin auth login</code>. Run <code>devin auth login</code> once in a terminal, and be aware that a Windsurf key in your environment takes precedence over that stored login. Devin Agent in BeanBot supports: - [[Editor Context->Automatic Context Capture]] Seamlessly injects the active editor state into agent prompts. - **[[MCP Tools]]**: Devin accepts a per-session MCP server, so BeanBot hands it the plugin's internal server automatically — no manual MCP registration is needed. - **Model Selection**: Exposed as an ACP config option, so the in-session model dropdown works. To pin a different default for every new session instead, pass <code>--model</code> under Process Arguments in <code>Options &gt; BeanBot</code>, or set `DEVIN_MODEL`. - **Agent / Mode List**: The agent selector is offered. - **Session List**: Sessions come from Devin itself, so the dropdown reflects its own list and needs no local tracking. - **Interleaved prompts**: a new message is sent immediately (it does not wait in the [[Queuing Messages]] toolbar queue). See [[Cursor Agent]] for the same style. - **Slash Commands**: Devin advertises its full slash-command set over the protocol, so its commands appear in the command palette with their descriptions and argument hints. Its account commands show up as <code>/login</code>, <code>/logout</code> and <code>/status</code>. #### Limitations - **Mode Switching**: Devin does not accept a mode change mid-session, so switching modes in an open session is not offered. Set the starting mode with the CLI's <code>--permission-mode</code> flag under Process Arguments instead. - **Cloud sessions**: <code>devin --cloud</code> drives a Devin Cloud session rather than the local agent. BeanBot connects to the ACP server, which is the local agent, so cloud features such as Playbooks, Secrets and Knowledge are not part of this integration. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Onboarding]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Queuing Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Copilot Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> #### Install - **All platforms (npm)**: `npm install -g @github/copilot` - **Windows (WinGet)**: `winget install GitHub.Copilot` - **macOS / Linux (Homebrew)**: `brew install --cask copilot-cli` - **macOS / Linux (script)**: `curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash` The npm install needs **Node.js 22 or later**. CLI docs: <a href="https://github.com/github/copilot-cli" target="_blank" rel="noopener">github.com/github/copilot-cli</a>. #### About <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/copilot-surfaces/copilot-cli" target="_blank" rel="noopener">GitHub Copilot CLI</a> is a terminal-native coding agent. Run <code>copilot --acp</code> and it acts as an **ACP server** over stdio: it speaks JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout and is meant to be spawned by an ACP-aware editor, so it is not a command to run yourself. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>copilot</code>, run with the launch argument <code>--acp</code>. **Authenticate first**: run <code>copilot login</code> once in a terminal (or use <code>/login</code> inside the CLI) with an active Copilot subscription. BeanBot cannot complete this for you. A fine-grained personal access token with the "Copilot Requests" permission also works via the `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN` or `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variables. Copilot Agent in BeanBot supports: - [[Editor Context->Automatic Context Capture]] the active editor state is attached to your prompts. - **[[MCP Tools]]**: Copilot accepts a per-session HTTP/SSE MCP server, so BeanBot hands it the plugin's internal server automatically — no manual MCP registration is needed. - **Model Selection**: exposed as an ACP config option, so the in-session model dropdown works. - **Agent / Mode List**: Copilot advertises three modes — **Agent**, **Plan** and **Autopilot** — and the selector is offered. - **Session List**: sessions come from Copilot itself, so the dropdown reflects its own list and needs no local tracking. A session is closed before it is reloaded, so a resume never replays against a session still holding work. - **[[Queuing Messages]]**: a new message is held and combined into the next prompt rather than interrupting the running turn. - **Slash Commands**: Copilot advertises its slash-command set over the protocol, so its commands appear in the command palette. #### Limitations - **Permissions**: Copilot exposes its own <code>allow&#95;all</code> permission config option. BeanBot drives mode and model through its own [[Permission Requests]] dialog and does not surface that toggle — leave <code>allow&#95;all</code> off if you want to review changes first. - **Mode switching** goes through the generic config-option method rather than <code>session/set&#95;mode</code>, so it works only where Copilot accepts a config change mid-session. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Onboarding]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Queuing Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Codex Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Install</div> All platforms: <pre><code>npm install -g @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp@2.2.2</code></pre> The package bundles the Codex CLI, so a separate `codex` install is not needed. The first session asks you to authenticate with a ChatGPT account or an <code>OPENAI&#95;API&#95;KEY</code>. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">About</div> <a href="https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/codex-acp" target="_blank" rel="noopener">codex-acp</a> is an ACP adapter that exposes OpenAI Codex over the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a>, which is what BeanBot speaks. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>codex-acp</code>. Codex Agent in BeanBot supports: - [[Editor Context->Automatic Context Capture]] the active editor state is attached to your prompts. - **[[MCP Tools]]**: codex-acp accepts a per-session HTTP MCP server, so BeanBot hands it the plugin's internal server automatically — no manual MCP registration is needed. - **Model Selection**: exposed as an ACP config option, so the in-session model dropdown works (reasoning effort rides along in the model id). - **Mode Switching**: the approval/sandbox presets (read-only, workspace-write, agent, full access) map to the in-session mode dropdown. - **[[Queuing Messages]]**: your message waits until the running turn ends before it is sent — Codex only accepts mid-turn steering through an extension BeanBot does not speak. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Plan Slideout</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> When the agent emits a plan — its step list for the task in hand — the steps appear in a slideout docked at the bottom of the message thread, above the input box and below the chat. It borrows height from the thread only, so the input area never shrinks. **Collapsed** the header shows the first unfinished step, its status icon and a `(done/total)` counter. **Expanded** it shows the full list under a `Plan (done/total)` title, up to eight rows at a time; a longer plan scrolls inside the slideout. Rows carry a pending, in-progress or completed icon: the active step is bold in the accent colour, completed steps are muted. The slideout opens automatically when a plan is first created or when the agent adds more steps. An update that keeps the same number of steps preserves whatever you last chose, so collapsing it does not make it reopen on every progress update. Starting or loading a session clears it. Click anywhere on the header — the title, the chevron, the counter or the progress bar — to collapse or expand it. The **×** button at the right end of the header closes the slideout; the dismissal is remembered for that session and plan, so reloading the session or a status-only progress update does not bring it back. A plan whose steps change opens the slideout again, and the state lasts for the current IDE session. > [[Thinking and Tool Responses]] > [[Pinned Messages]] > [[Chat Features]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Kilo Code Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> #### Install - **macOS (Homebrew)**: `brew install Kilo-Org/tap/kilo` - **Linux / WSL (install script)**: `curl -fsSL https://kilo.ai/cli/install | bash` - **Windows (npm)**: `npm install -g @kilocode/cli` The install script puts the binary in `~/.kilo/bin`; the Homebrew tap brings its own runtime. The npm route needs Node.js on your `PATH`. CLI docs: <a href="https://kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/platforms/cli" target="_blank" rel="noopener">kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/platforms/cli</a>. #### About <a href="https://kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/platforms/cli" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Kilo Code</a> is an OpenCode-derived coding agent. Running <code>kilo acp</code> makes it act as an **ACP server** over stdio: it speaks JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout and is meant to be spawned by an ACP-aware editor, so it is not a command to run yourself. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>kilo</code> — the alias <code>kilocode</code> is detected too — run with the default launch argument <code>acp</code>. **Authentication** is worth setting up before you connect: run <code>kilo auth login</code> in a terminal, or start <code>kilo</code> on its own and use <code>/connect</code> inside it. MCP servers are handed to Kilo per session with their headers forwarded, so no manual registration is needed. Kilo Code in BeanBot supports: - [[Editor Context->Automatic Context Capture]] Seamlessly injects the active editor state into agent prompts. - **[[MCP Tools]]**: Kilo accepts a per-session MCP server, so BeanBot hands it the plugin's internal HTTP server automatically — no manual registration is needed. - **Model Selection**: Exposed as an ACP config option, so the in-session model dropdown works. - **Thinking Level**: Kilo reports each model's variants as a separate `effort` config option, so the thinking-level dropdown works with it. - **Agent / Mode List**: The agent selector is offered, and mode changes go through the protocol's mode request, so the dropdown works in an open session. - **Session List**: Sessions come from Kilo itself, so the dropdown reflects its own list and needs no local tracking. - **Queued messages**: a second message sent while a turn is running waits in the [[Queuing Messages]] toolbar queue and is delivered after the current turn ends. - **Slash Commands**: Kilo advertises its slash-command set over the protocol, so its commands appear in the command palette with their descriptions. #### Limitations - **Queued messages**: Kilo can accept a follow-up prompt while a turn runs and hands it off at its next step, but BeanBot deliberately holds the message until the turn ends (see [[Queuing Messages]]) so a running turn is never cut short as superseded. Interleaved agents such as [[OpenCode]] send immediately instead. - **Model switching path**: BeanBot changes the model through Kilo's `model` config option and the thinking level through `effort`, rather than the dedicated (unstable) model request. Both dropdowns show the options Kilo reports back, not a fixed list. - **Node.js for the npm route**: the Windows install command uses npm, so it needs Node.js installed; the install script and Homebrew tap do not. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Onboarding]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Queuing Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Cline Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> #### Install - **macOS / Linux / WSL**: `npm i -g cline` - **Windows (PowerShell, CMD or Git Bash)**: `npm i -g cline` The npm route requires **Node.js**, and BeanBot needs Cline CLI **3.0.74 or newer** (`npm i -g cline@latest`). Older 2.x builds expose an ACP server without `session/load`, `session/cancel` or config options, so upgrade before connecting. CLI docs: <a href="https://docs.cline.bot/usage/acp" target="_blank" rel="noopener">docs.cline.bot/usage/acp</a>. #### About <a href="https://docs.cline.bot/usage/acp" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cline</a> is an open-source coding agent. Running <code>cline --acp</code> makes it act as an **ACP server** over stdio: it speaks JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout and is meant to be spawned by an ACP-aware editor, so it is not a command to run yourself. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>cline</code>, run with the default launch argument <code>--acp</code>. **Authentication** is a CLI prerequisite: run <code>cline auth</code> once in a terminal (or export <code>CLINE&#95;API&#95;KEY</code>) before connecting. Cline does expose ACP authenticate methods (Cline, ClinePass, ChatGPT subscription), but BeanBot has no in-chat sign-in, so a fresh install without credentials fails <code>session/new</code> with an authentication error — sign in first, then pick Cline in the chooser. Cline in BeanBot supports: - [[Editor Context->Automatic Context Capture]] Seamlessly injects the active editor state into agent prompts. - **Model Selection**: Exposed as an ACP config option, so the in-session model dropdown works. - **Plan / Act mode**: The agent selector is offered and sends <code>session/set&#95;mode</code>, but Cline applies the chosen mode when it creates the session manager (on the first prompt). Pick the mode before the first message, or start a new session after changing it. - **Queued messages**: a message sent while a turn is running is held in the [[Queuing Messages]] toolbar queue until the turn ends. Cline accepts the second prompt but resolves it with <code>end&#95;turn</code> immediately while the first turn keeps streaming, so sending immediately would unlock the input against a running turn. - **Session reload**: with Cline CLI 3.0.74+ sessions can be resumed with <code>session/load</code>, so [[Reloading a Session]] works for sessions Cline has already persisted. Older 2.x builds do not implement the method; reload is refused and the status line asks you to upgrade. #### Limitations The harness chooser labels Cline <b>Limited</b>; the items below are what that badge points to. See [[Onboarding]]. - **No plugin MCP tools**: BeanBot does not hand its internal MCP server to Cline (it sends an empty list); the embedded server may still run for other harnesses. Configure MCP servers in Cline's own configuration if you need them. - **No session list from Cline**: Cline does not implement <code>session/list</code>, so the session dropdown only shows sessions tracked locally by this BeanBot instance — sessions created in another Cline client do not appear. - **No token statistics**: Cline sends no usage updates, so per-turn token and cost figures stay empty for this harness; see [[Check token usage]]. - **Thinking level**: there is no thinking config option. Add <code>--thinking &lt;level&gt;</code> after the existing <code>--acp</code> argument under Process Arguments in <code>Options &gt; BeanBot</code>, or set it in the CLI, to influence reasoning before a session starts. - **Images and binary attachments are dropped**: Cline advertises image prompts but its ACP <code>prompt()</code> reads only text blocks, so image blocks and binary <code>resource&#95;link</code> blocks never reach the model. Text attachments are inlined as text blocks and do work — see [[Attachments]]. - **No in-chat sign-in**: BeanBot has no ACP authenticate client for Cline; credentials must exist before the connection. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Onboarding]] > [[Queuing Messages]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Options Panel Reference]]<div style="display: flex;
